danish.title: Sjette bog (1808–10) — Kapitel 8
paragraphs: Atter blev Pierre grebet af den tungsindighed, han så meget frygtede. I tre dage efter sin tale i logen lå han på en sofa hjemme, tog ikke imod nogen og gik ingen steder.
Netop da modtog han et brev fra sin kone, der tryglende bad ham om at se hende, fortalte ham, hvor bedrøvet hun var over ham, og hvor meget hun ønskede at vie hele sit liv til ham.
I slutningen af brevet meddelte hun, at hun om få dage ville vende tilbage til Petersborg fra udlandet.

I kølvandet på dette brev trængte en af frimurerbrødrene, Pierre satte mindre pris på end de andre, sig ind til ham, og idet han drejede samtalen hen på Pierres ægteskabsforhold, udtrykte han som broderligt råd den mening, at hans strenghed over for sin kone var forkert, og at han forsømte en af frimureriets allerførste regler ved ikke at tilgive den angrende.

Samtidig sendte hans svigermor, fyrst Vasilijs hustru, bud til ham med bøn om at komme, blot for et øjeblik, for at drøfte et yderst vigtigt anliggende. Pierre indså, at der var en sammensværgelse imod ham, og at de ville genforene ham med hans kone, og i hans daværende stemning var dette ikke engang ham ubehageligt. Intet betød noget for ham. Intet i livet syntes ham af stor vigtighed, og under indflydelse af den tungsindighed, der beherskede ham, satte han hverken pris på sin frihed eller sin beslutning om at straffe sin kone.
»Ingen har ret, og ingen har skyld, og altså er hun heller ikke skyldig,« tænkte han.

Hvis han ikke straks gav sit samtykke til en genforening med sin kone, var det kun fordi han i sin tungsindige tilstand ikke følte sig i stand til at tage nogen beslutning. Var hans kone kommet til ham, ville han ikke have afvist hende. Sammenlignet med det, der optog ham, var det vel ligegyldigt, om han levede med sin kone eller ej?
Uden at svare hverken sin kone eller sin svigermor forberedte Pierre sig sent en aften på en rejse og tog af sted til Moskva for at opsøge Josef Aleksejevitj. Her er, hvad han noterede i sin dagbog:
Moskva, den 17. november

Jeg er netop vendt tilbage fra min velgører og skynder mig at skrive ned, hvad jeg har oplevet. Josef Aleksejevitj lever fattigt og har i tre år lidt af en smertefuld blæresygdom. Ingen har nogensinde hørt ham klage med et suk eller et ord. Fra morgen til sen aften, når han ikke spiser sin yderst tarvelige mad, arbejder han med videnskaben. Han modtog mig nådigt og bad mig sætte mig på sengen, hvor han lå. Jeg gjorde Østens og Jerusalems Ridderes tegn, og han svarede på samme måde og spurgte mig med et mildt smil, hvad jeg havde lært og vundet i de preussiske og skotske loger. Jeg fortalte ham alt så godt jeg kunne, herunder hvad jeg havde foreslået vores petersborgske loge, den dårlige modtagelse og mit brud med brødrene. Josef Aleksejevitj, der længe var forblevet tavs og eftertænksom, fortalte mig sit syn på sagen, som straks oplyste hele min fortid og den fremtidige vej, jeg burde følge. Han overraskede mig ved at spørge, om jeg huskede ordenens tredobbelte mål: (1) Bevarelse og studium af mysteriet. (2) Selvrenselse og selvreformation som forberedelse til at modtage det. Og (3) Forbedring af menneskeslægten ved stræben efter en sådan renselse. Hvilket er det vigtigste af disse tre? Selvfølgelig selvreformationen og selvrenselsen. Kun dette mål kan vi altid stræbe efter uafhængigt af omstændighederne. Men netop dette mål kræver de største anstrengelser af os; og derfor mister vi, vildledt af stolthed, dette mål af syne og beskæftiger os enten med mysteriet, som vi i vores urenhed er uværdige til at modtage, eller søger at forbedre menneskeslægten, mens vi selv er eksempler på nederdrægtighed og udsvævelse. Illuminismen er ikke en ren lære, netop fordi den tiltrækkes af social aktivisme og oppustes af stolthed. På dette grundlag fordømte Josef Aleksejevitj min tale og hele min virksomhed, og i min sjæls dyb gav jeg ham ret. Da han talte om mine familieforhold, sagde han: »En sand frimurers fornemste pligt, som jeg har fortalt dig, ligger i at fuldkommengøre sig selv. Vi tror ofte, at vi hurtigere når vores mål ved at fjerne alle livets vanskeligheder, men tværtimod, kære ven, er det kun midt i verdslige bekymringer, vi kan nå vore tre hovedmål: (1) Selvkendskab — for mennesket kan kun kende sig selv ved sammenligning, (2) Selvfuldkommenhed, der kun kan opnås gennem kamp, og (3) Opnåelse af den fornemste dyd — kærligheden til døden. Kun livets omskiftelser kan vise os dets tomhed og udvikle vores medfødte kærlighed til døden eller til genfødsel i et nyt liv.« Disse ord er desto mere bemærkelsesværdige, fordi Josef Aleksejevitj til trods for sine store fysiske lidelser aldrig er livstræt, skønt han elsker døden, som han — trods sin indre mands renhed og ophøjethed — endnu ikke føler sig tilstrækkelig forberedt på. Min velgører forklarede mig derpå fuldt ud betydningen af Skabelsens Store Kvadrat og påpegede, at tallene tre og syv er grundlaget for alt. Han rådede mig til ikke at undgå omgang med Petersborgs brødre, men kun at påtage mig poster af anden rang i logen og forsøge, mens jeg afledte brødrene fra stolthed, at vende dem mod den sande vej — selvkendskab og selvfuldkommenhed. Desuden rådede han mig personligt frem for alt at holde vagt over mig selv, og i den hensigt gav han mig en notesbog — den jeg nu skriver i — og hvori jeg fremover vil notere alle mine handlinger.
Petersborg, den 23. november

Jeg lever atter med min kone. Min svigermor kom grædende til mig og sagde, at Hélène var her, og at hun bønfaldt mig om at høre hende; at hun var uskyldig og ulykkelig over min forladelse, og meget mere. Jeg vidste, at hvis jeg blot lod mig se hende, ville jeg ikke have kræfter til at blive ved med at nægte hende, hvad hun ønskede. I min rådvildhed vidste jeg ikke, hvem jeg skulle søge hjælp og råd hos. Havde min velgører været her, ville han have fortalt mig, hvad jeg skulle gøre. Jeg gik op på mit værelse og genlæste Josef Aleksejevitjs breve og mindedes mine samtaler med ham, og af alt dette udledte jeg, at jeg ikke bør afvise en bønfaldende og bør række en hjælpende hånd til enhver — især til en, der er mig så nært knyttet — og at jeg må bære mit kors. Men hvis jeg tilgiver hende for det godes skyld, så lad foreningen med hende kun have et åndeligt formål. Det var, hvad jeg besluttede, og hvad jeg skrev til Josef Aleksejevitj. Jeg sagde min kone, at jeg bad hende glemme fortiden, tilgive mig, hvad ondt jeg måtte have gjort hende, og at jeg intet havde at tilgive. Det glædede mig at sige hende dette. Hun behøver ikke vide, hvor svært det var for mig at se hende igen. Jeg har indrettet mig på øverste etage af dette store hus og oplever en lykkelig følelse af genfødsel.

english.title: Book Six (1808 - 10) — Chapter 8
paragraphs: Once again Pierre was overtaken by the depression he dreaded so much. For three days after delivering his speech at the lodge, he lay on a sofa at home, seeing no one and going nowhere.
It was just then that he received a letter from his wife, who begged him to see her, telling him how upset she was about him and how she wished to devote her whole life to him.
At the end of the letter she informed him that she would be returning to Petersburg from abroad in a few days.

Shortly after this letter, one of the Masonic Brothers whom Pierre respected less than the others forced his way in to see him. Turning the conversation to Pierre's marriage, he offered some brotherly advice, suggesting that Pierre's harshness toward his wife was wrong and that he was violating one of the fundamental rules of Freemasonry by refusing to forgive the repentant.

At the same time his mother-in-law, Prince Vasili's wife, sent word begging him to come, if only for a few minutes, to discuss an extremely important matter. Pierre could see there was a conspiracy against him and that they wanted to reunite him with his wife, but in his current state of mind, this wasn't even unpleasant to him. Nothing mattered to him. Nothing in life seemed particularly important, and under the weight of the depression that gripped him, he valued neither his freedom nor his determination to punish his wife.
"No one is right and no one is to blame; so she too is not to blame," he thought.

If he didn't immediately agree to a reunion with his wife, it was only because in his depressed state he didn't feel capable of taking any step at all. Had his wife simply come to him, he wouldn't have turned her away. Compared to what was preoccupying him, did it really matter whether he lived with his wife or not?
Without replying to either his wife or his mother-in-law, Pierre set out late one night for Moscow to see Joseph Alexeevich. This is what he wrote in his diary:
Moscow, 17th November

I have just returned from my benefactor and hasten to write down what I experienced. Joseph Alexeevich is living in poverty and has been suffering for three years from a painful bladder disease. No one has ever heard him groan or utter a word of complaint. From morning till late at night, except when he eats his very plain food, he works on his studies. He received me warmly and had me sit on the bed where he lay. I made the sign of the Knights of the East and of Jerusalem, and he responded in kind, asking me with a gentle smile what I had learned and gained in the Prussian and Scottish lodges. I told him everything as best I could, including what I had proposed to our Petersburg lodge, the poor reception I had met with, and my break with the Brothers. Joseph Alexeevich, after remaining silent and thoughtful for a long while, shared his view of the matter, which immediately illuminated my entire past and the future path I should follow. He surprised me by asking whether I remembered the threefold aim of the order: (1) The preservation and study of the mystery. (2) The purification and reformation of oneself for its reception, and (3) The improvement of the human race by striving for such purification. Which is the principal aim of these three? Certainly self-reformation and self-purification. Only toward this aim can we always strive, regardless of circumstances. But at the same time, this very aim demands the greatest efforts from us; and so, led astray by pride, losing sight of this aim, we occupy ourselves either with the mystery — which in our impurity we are unworthy to receive — or seek to reform the human race while ourselves setting an example of baseness and depravity. Illuminism is not a pure doctrine, precisely because it is attracted to social activism and inflated by pride. On these grounds Joseph Alexeevich condemned my speech and my entire course of action, and in the depths of my soul I agreed with him. Speaking of my family affairs he said to me: "The chief duty of a true Mason, as I have told you, lies in perfecting himself. We often think that by removing all the difficulties from our lives we will reach our goal more quickly, but on the contrary, my dear sir, it is only in the midst of worldly cares that we can achieve our three chief aims: (1) Self-knowledge — for man can only know himself through comparison, (2) Self-perfecting, which can only be attained through struggle, and (3) The attainment of the chief virtue — love of death. Only the trials of life can reveal its vanity and nurture our innate love of death, or of rebirth to a new life." These words are all the more remarkable because, despite his great physical suffering, Joseph Alexeevich never tires of life, though he loves death — for which, in spite of the purity and loftiness of his inner being, he does not yet feel himself sufficiently prepared. My benefactor then explained to me in full the meaning of the Great Square of creation and pointed out that the numbers three and seven are the foundation of everything. He advised me not to withdraw from the Petersburg Brothers, but to take only second-rank positions in the lodge, and to try, while steering the Brothers away from pride, to turn them toward the true path of self-knowledge and self-perfecting. Besides this, he advised me personally above all to keep watch over myself, and to that end he gave me a notebook — the one I am now writing in — in which I will henceforth record all my actions.
Petersburg, 23rd November

I am living with my wife again. My mother-in-law came to me in tears and said that Helene was here and begged me to hear her; that she was innocent and miserable at my desertion, and much more. I knew that if I once let myself see her I wouldn't have the strength to keep refusing what she wanted. In my confusion I didn't know whose aid or advice to seek. Had my benefactor been here he would have told me what to do. I went to my room and reread Joseph Alexeevich's letters and recalled my conversations with him, and from all of it concluded that I must not refuse someone who comes asking for help, and must extend a hand to everyone — especially to one so closely bound to me — and that I must bear my cross. But if I forgive her for the sake of doing right, then let our reunion serve only a spiritual purpose. That is what I decided, and what I wrote to Joseph Alexeevich. I told my wife that I asked her to forget the past, to forgive me whatever wrong I may have done her, and that I had nothing to forgive. It gave me joy to tell her this. She need not know how hard it was for me to see her again. I have settled on the upper floor of this big house and am feeling a happy sense of renewal.
